data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
inflation_management: Iran has lived with chronic high inflation driven by sanctions, monetized deficits, and repeated currency collapses, with no credible nominal anchor. Inflation ran 12-33% through 2006-14 (peaking at 32.9% in 2013 after subsidy reform and sanctions), moderated briefly to 6.8% in 2016 after the JCPOA, then exploded again: 40.2% in 2021, 45.8% in 2022, and a projected 50.9% in 2025, the series high. The rial's parallel-market collapse is the transmission mechanism, and central bank financing of the budget entrenches expectations. Inflation control is subordinate to sanctions politics.
debt_management: Paradoxically, measured public debt is moderate: it was just 15.2% of GDP in 2006, stayed low through the oil boom, jumped to 45.9% in 2016 on GDP rebasing effects, and the IMF projects 37.3% for 2025. Sanctions cut Iran off from borrowing, so deficits were monetized (hence inflation) rather than debt-financed. GDP in dollar terms collapsed from $722.1bn in 2011 to $209.5bn in 2020 on sanctions and the rial's fall, recovering only to a projected $371.2bn in 2025. The binding constraint is inflation and external isolation, not the debt ratio.

key_events.event: Tightened US/EU sanctions over the nuclear program; rial collapsed and inflation hit 29-33%.
JCPOA nuclear deal signed; sanctions relief followed in 2016 and inflation fell to 6.8%.
US withdrew from the JCPOA and reimposed sanctions; rial plunged and inflation surged past 25%.
Fuel-price protests; COVID-19 and 'maximum pressure' crushed oil exports and GDP.
Mahsa Amini protests after her death in custody; inflation hit 45.8%.
Regional conflict escalation and continued sanctions kept inflation near 50% in the 2025 projection.

outlook_next_decade: Iran's economy will remain hostage to geopolitics: sanctions relief would unlock oil exports, investment, and disinflation, while continued confrontation keeps inflation high and growth stagnant. Domestic capacity in manufacturing and a young population offer upside under any opening. Analytical assessment must be heavily caveated: outcomes range from reintegration-driven recovery to further isolation and currency crisis, and data quality is weak. Debt is not the binding constraint; the exchange rate and inflation are.
caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
